books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the report of the Hartford Convention, January 1815: In December 1814, as diplomats negotiated an end to the War of 1812, Federalist delegates from New England met at Hartford, Connecticut, to protest the war and the power of the Democratic-Republican government. A few radical delegates talked of New England leaving the Union, but the convention rejected secession. Instead it proposed amendments to the Constitution, including requiring a two-thirds vote of Congress to declare war, to admit new states, or to restrict trade, and barring two presidents in a row from the same state. The convention sent delegates to Washington to present its demands, and arrived just as news came that the war had ended.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Report of the Hartford Convention, January 1815. Paraphrased, not quoted; public domain source.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The Hartford Convention is most significant in American politics because it

options.text: won New England the right to secede from the Union
options.misconception: Secession was talked about but rejected at the convention.

options.text: forced Congress to adopt all of its proposed amendments
options.misconception: None of the amendments were adopted.

options.text: made the Federalist Party look disloyal and helped destroy it
ended the War of 1812 on terms favorable to Britain
options.misconception: The war ended at Ghent, not at Hartford.

rationales.A: A few radical delegates raised secession, but the convention rejected it and proposed amendments instead. No right to secede was won.
rationales.B: The delegates carried their amendments to Washington, but Congress adopted none of them. The proposals died with the party.
rationales.C: The delegates arrived in Washington just as news came that the war had ended in an American victory. Meeting to protest a war that was already won made the Federalists look disloyal, and their national party dissolved soon after.
rationales.D: The Treaty of Ghent ended the war, and Hartford had no part in it. The convention's significance is what it did to the Federalists, not to the peace.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the convention did. It protested a war that was about to end in an American victory.
2. Ask how that looked. Delegates demanding limits on the government while the nation celebrated a victory looked disloyal.
3. Put it together. The timing turned a protest into a reputation for treason, and the party never recovered.
Background: The Federalist Party had opposed the war from the start, and the Hartford meeting was its last act as a national party.
Remember: when a protest arrives just as its cause disappears, ask what it does to the protesters' reputation.
